title: Vector Components & Decomposition - High Yield Guide
summary: Vectors in a Cartesian coordinate system can be uniquely resolved into perpendicular components along the coordinate axes.
key_formulas: Fx = |F| * cos(θ) (when θ is measured from the positive x-axis)
Fy = |F| * sin(θ) (when θ is measured from the positive x-axis)
θ = arctan(|Fy / Fx|) adjusted for quadrant signs: Quadrant I (θ), II (180° - α), III (180° + α), IV (360° - α)
common_pitfalls: Always check which axis the angle θ is adjacent to. If the angle is measured from the vertical (y-axis), the components invert: Fy = F cos(θ) and Fx = F sin(θ).
Assign quadrant signs explicitly: Q1 (+,+), Q2 (-,+), Q3 (-,-), Q4 (+,-). Trigonometric functions alone may lose quadrant sign context if you only use acute reference angles.
worked_example: A force of 20 N acts at 30° above the negative x-axis (Quadrant 2). Components: Fx = -20 * cos(30°) = -10√3 N ≈ -17.32 N. Fy = +20 * sin(30°) = +10 N.

title: Vector Addition & Resultants - High Yield Guide
summary: Vectors must be combined using vector algebra, not simple arithmetic addition of magnitudes.
key_formulas: Component-wise addition: Rx = Ax + Bx + Cx + ..., Ry = Ay + By + Cy + ...
Parallelogram Law (2 vectors at angle θ): R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
common_pitfalls: Do not add magnitudes directly unless vectors are strictly collinear in the same direction (θ = 0°).
Remember that cos(120°) = -0.5 and cos(180°) = -1. When two equal vectors of magnitude A act at 120°, their resultant magnitude is also A.
worked_example: Given A = 3i + 4j and B = 5i - 2j. Resultant R = A + B = (3+5)i + (4-2)j = 8i + 2j. Magnitude |R| = √(64 + 4) = √68 ≈ 8.25 units.

title: 1D Motion with Constant Acceleration - High Yield Guide
summary: When acceleration is constant along a straight line, kinematic equations relate displacement (s), initial velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), and time (t).
key_formulas: s = ut + 0.5 * a * t² (no final velocity v)
s = ((u + v) / 2) * t (average velocity formulation for constant a)
common_pitfalls: Deceleration: acceleration vector is opposite to velocity. If moving along +x, deceleration means 'a' is negative.
Vertical motion under gravity: with upwards as positive, acceleration is a = -g (e.g. -9.8 m/s² or -10 m/s²). At maximum height, v = 0.
Always identify the missing variable among (u, v, a, s, t) to select the single direct kinematic equation.
worked_example: A ball thrown upward with u = 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). Maximum height: v² = u² - 2gh => 0 = 400 - 20h => h = 20 m.
